definition: Parametric programming is a type of mathematical optimization, where the optimization problem is solved as a function of one or multiple parameters.
details: Developed in parallel to sensitivity analysis, its earliest mention can be found in a thesis from 1952. Since then, there have been considerable developments for the cases of multiple parameters, presence of integer variables as well as nonlinearities.

explainer.lead: Parametric programming is a type of mathematical optimization in which the problem is solved as a function of one or multiple parameters. It matters because a single solution then covers a whole range of parameter values rather than one fixed instance.

tiers.eli5: Instead of solving one puzzle, you work out the answer for every version of the puzzle as one ingredient changes.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it when a model's data or coefficients vary, solving once to get the solution as a function of the parameter. A pitfall is that multiple parameters, integer variables, and nonlinearities make the problem considerably harder.
tiers.paperLevel: Parametric programming solves an optimization problem as a function of one or multiple parameters; developed alongside sensitivity analysis with earliest mention in a 1952 thesis, it has since seen considerable development for multiple parameters, integer variables, and nonlinearities.

explainer.example: Rather than re-solving a linear program for every possible budget, parametric programming yields the optimal solution as a function of the budget parameter over its range.
